text: What could actually harm a patient?

text: Dora could miss a red flag symptom, such as sudden vision loss or severe pain.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: The patient could be distressed, and Dora just ignores it and carries on without actually acknowledging the distress.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: There's many, many, many documented hazards of these, 20, 30, 40, and we have to ensure that none of them actually happen in real life.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: So how would we actually normally catch a problem like this before it actually spreads?
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: We would lean usually on the playbook that most software ships on.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: You ship to a small percentage of people, you watch the dashboard, you roll back if it breaks, and you iterate from there.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: This is a very good playbook.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: It's reactive, it's fast, it's very safe, and it's how the industry usually de-risks the launch.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: But there's a hidden assumption here that it only works because you can afford to be wrong for an instant.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: A bad change hits a few users, you can quickly catch it, you can roll back, and no one's actually literally harmed.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: This is the one assumption is why that it breaks when the actual user is a patient.

text: For 5%, that could be a hundreds, if not thousands of patients that have got unproven changes and undue care.

text: So how do you iterate at all when you can't touch a patient until you're sure?
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: Well, for this, we started looking at examples from other high-reliable industries.

speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: They put millions of miles of simulations first before they actually got any passages into the car.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: For us, we believe in the same thing.

text: Simulation is only the real ethical option we can go with.

text: You can't run all the hazards I just mentioned on real people as a first grasp.

text: So for our clinical history taking, we built a simulation framework called Matrix.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: And I'm going to work through how it works and how we use it to prove that our product is safe.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: And the paper's on Archive if you want to read it along with some of the other research that we do.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: At its core, Matrix recreates a real clinical conversation but with no real patient in it.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: We use an LLM to play the patient.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: We call it Patbot.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: And what does it do?
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: We use a simulated patient and not a hired actor because hired actors don't scale.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: If we want to iterate very fast and simulate different things at the same time while also updating our system, hiring actors would just be too slow of a process.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: So as a first version, we just use a simulated patient.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: The simulated patient is conditioned on the actual scenario we want to test.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: The scenario defines exactly what the patient should try and do when talking to our agent.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: For example, asking whether the agent is a human or an AI.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: Patbot then has a conversation with Dora, our target system, and then generates simulated dialogues.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: Very importantly, this all happens under a very specific clinical use case context.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: So the scenarios are grounded in real clinical workflows and not abstract situations.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: So how do we actually make sure that the patient is realistic?
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: If Patbot is sounding robotic, the tests aren't really worth much.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: So we had to, of course, validate it.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: The first thing we did was just a pure script adherence check.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: If we told Patbot to do something, does Patbot do it?
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: Yes or no?
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: This helped us filter out a lot of maybe weaker models that didn't listen to instructions properly.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: But just purely following instructions does not make a realistic patient.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: We want a patient that flows more realistically like a real person.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: So we set up what's called a PPI study, a patient and public involvement study.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: We took real patients and we showed them two sets of conversations.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: One conversation was between a real doctor and a real patient, and one conversation was between Dora and Papot within our matrix framework.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: And we showed them these two examples side by side and said, looking at the patient, can you tell which one is the real person and which one is the simulated person?

text: OK.

text: I think us as engineers sometimes are pretty good at finding these things, but it was actually much more difficult than we thought.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: And we did this with four conversation sets, basically.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: In three out of the four, the majority of people actually thought that the simulated patient was more realistic.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: But the most important thing that we found was, of course, there is no single realistic patient.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: That doesn't really make sense.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: Some people prefer to speak more verbosely, a lot of ums and ahs.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: Some people are more straight to the point, a lot of yeses and nos.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: But the point is that we actually want to simulate all these different scenarios.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: We want to simulate people with very diverse personas.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: But what it did show us is that at least our PadBot was realistic enough for this simulation.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: OK, so now you've got thousands and thousands of simulated dialogues.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: Are us as the engineers going to go read through them one by one and see if a hazard happened?
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: Of course not.

speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: And number two, we're on clinicians, so we don't actually know if an actual hazard has really occurred.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: So we use another LLM as a judge, of course, and we call it Bevjudge.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: It takes the simulated dialogue.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: A set of expected behaviors and the hazardous scenarios that we talk through with clinicians, and it makes a judgment pass or fail.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: So we get a structured output of which hazards were triggered and what actually went wrong in that scenario.

text: So how did we validate BevJudge?
speaker: SPEAKER_00

speaker: SPEAKER_00

speaker: SPEAKER_00

speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: You would rather over-call hazards that aren't there than under-call hazards that are there.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: So now we have an automated judge that performs at expert level, and this is actually what makes this whole process scalable.

text: So how do you do this without experimenting on the patient?
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: The answer isn't like maybe very long ago in our world, eight months ago, we would manually prompt engineer this.

text: We would look at which agents are going wrong or which prompts are going wrong, and we would have to manually prompt engineer.

text: But we know that prompt brittleness is real, and it's quite absurd.

text: Formatting changes alone have been seen to swing benchmark by 76 percentage points, and reordering few-shot examples flips a model from near-random, so near 50%, to near-state-of-the-art on some benchmarks.

text: And hand-tuning can't survive that.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: It's very subjective, it's not reproducible, and very importantly, it's extremely time-consuming.

text: So over the last year or so, there's been these prompt optimizers that have started to come out, and we've focused on those.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: The one that we use the most is JEPA, which stands for Genetic Pareto.

text: It comes from the same people who made DSPY, if anyone knows about them.

text: And how does JEPA work?
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: You essentially define a metric for what good is, which I'll get into a bit later.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: Then you pass your data through
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: Through Jepa and it tells you which examples failed.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: Then you get a very strong LLM to reflect on the failures and update the prompt automatically.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: You do this over and over and over again and it keeps what they call a Pareto frontier of the best prompts until your budget has been exhausted and you've now come up with what Jepa comes up with the best prompt.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: So we believe this is a much better process from both a time-consuming process, you know, it takes maybe manual prompt engineering, we're taking the order of hours to days, to this is an hour of minutes.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: And very importantly, it's reproducible, and there's a very clear order trail and clear feedback loop.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: And if anything goes wrong, you can just maybe it's purely now a data science problem.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: It's mainly focused on the data, how to make your data route, the feature engineering, and you define the actual metric along with the clinicians.

speaker: SPEAKER_00
